elements.char: the synaptic currents extracted from the LIF network as well. Including slower synapses, such
elements.label: text

elements.char: as NMDA synapses in the model setup, will on the other hand affect the LFP frequency con-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tent, particularly at low frequencies. This effect could be captured by a proxy including NMDA
elements.label: text

elements.char: in the sum of synaptic currents with a weight depending on the number and spatial distribution
elements.label: text

elements.char: of NMDA synapses. As with the synaptic weight distributions discussed above, the inclusion of
elements.label: text

elements.char: NMDA synapses when computing the LFP proxy presupposes that it is also included in the LIF
elements.label: text

elements.char: network model (which was beyond the scope of this study). Moreover, we did not model sub-
elements.label: text

elements.char: threshold active dendritic conductance [55], nor the active channels behind spike generation.
elements.label: text

elements.char: The contributions from the latter is expectedly negligible for at least the low frequencies of the
elements.label: text

elements.char: LFP [56] (but see [57
elements.label: text

elements.char: 59]), while the effect of the former should be explored in future projects.
elements.label: text

elements.char: The present suggested proxy assumes the LFP contribution following spikes to be spatio-
elements.label: text

elements.char: temporally separable, i.e., factorizable into a product of a function of time with a function of
elements.label: text

elements.char: space [30]. Due to, for example, the intrinsic filtering effect [29,36,60] this is not strictly true as
elements.label: text

elements.char: the spatial distribution of the transmembrane currents setting up the LFP depends to some
elements.label: text

elements.char: extent on the frequency. However, if warranted the present proxy can be extended, for example
elements.label: text

elements.char: by assuming a more detailed proxy consisting of a sum of such spatiotemporally separable
elements.label: text

elements.char: kernels.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Importance of this work for analytical studies of LFPs
elements.label: text

elements.char: Recently, we presented an analytical method to estimate the LFP spectrum from the dynamics
elements.label: text

elements.char: of a LIF network [61] using as LFP proxy the sum of the absolute values of synaptic currents.
elements.label: text

elements.char: By fitting a recurrent excitatory-inhibitory LIF network model to LFP recordings from mon-
elements.label: text

elements.char: keys presented with visual stimuli, we were able to estimate the LIF model that best fitted the
elements.label: text

elements.char: observed LFP, and to predict at least in part the observed firing rate and some of the visual fea-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tures in the receptive field that elicited the observed neural activity. In this recent work [61],
elements.label: text

elements.char: the time evolution of the LFP was computed analytically from the LIF network as a function of
elements.label: text

elements.char: the external input by applying linear response theory to the mean-field approximations of each
elements.label: text

elements.char: kind of synaptic current separately and then summing their absolute values over pyramidal
elements.label: text

elements.char: neurons (as in [15] and in Eq 2). In principle, it is possible to extend this analytical calculation
elements.label: text

elements.char: by using the more efficient proxy presented here by simply changing the coefficients in the
elements.label: text

elements.char: final sum of the synaptic currents. This paves the work for obtaining realistic analytical estima-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tions of LFPs from recurrent LIF networks. As discussed in [35], an efficient analytical
elements.label: text

elements.char: approach could be at the heart of the development of model-based analysis methods for per-
elements.label: text

elements.char: forming inferential statistics of network models on LFPs, analogous to the role played by
elements.label: text

elements.char: Dynamic Causal Modelling [62,63] in the analysis of EEG and fMRI recordings.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Outlook
elements.label: text

elements.char: Here we studied proxies for the LFP produced by a local 3D network, corresponding to a single
elements.label: text

elements.char: cortical layer. Experimentally recorded LFPs, however, are most likely containing contributions
elements.label: text

elements.char: from several layers [20]. Therefore, a natural extension of this work would be to study the LFP
elements.label: text

elements.char: generated by several connected 3D networks forming a full cortical columns [64,65] and deter-
elements.label: text

elements.char: mine how LFP proxies should be designed in this context. Since electrical potentials in the ner-
elements.label: text

elements.char: vous tissue are assumed to add linearly, we expect LFP proxies to be constructed in largely the
elements.label: text

elements.char: same manner as presented here, by summing synaptic contributions from different cortical lay-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ers, possibly with a weighting depending on the recording depths. Constructing the LFP signal
elements.label: text

elements.char: from a full cortical column model [65] is the topic for a separate ongoing project [66].
elements.label: text

elements.char: We expect our proxy to also work well for other brain structures where pyramidal neurons
elements.label: text

elements.char: are elongated and arranged in an almost parallel way, such as the CA1 and CA2 regions of the
elements.label: text

elements.char: LFP Proxy for Integrate-and-Fire Networks
